title: Black Holes
subtitle: Horizons, shadows, and extreme gravity
description: Interactive exhibit on black holes: event horizons, scale, approach regions, illustrative lensing, accretion appearance, tidal forces, EHT imaging, and how astronomers detect them.
source_note: Scientific outreach. Scale, approach, and lensing labs are ILLUSTRATIVE. Schwarzschild-radius numbers assume a non-rotating (Schwarzschild) model unless noted; real astrophysical black holes can rotate (Kerr). EHT images are interferometric reconstructions, not photographs of a solid black surface.
illustrative_disclaimer: ILLUSTRATIVE — EDUCATIONAL SIMPLIFICATION. Diagrams are not exact Kerr ray-tracing unless separately labeled as simulation. The photon sphere is not a solid shell. Observers cannot hover freely at the event horizon.

classification_legend.reconstruction: Images or maps reconstructed from interferometric/survey data (e.g. EHT)
classification_legend.theoretical_model: Classical GR concept (e.g. Schwarzschild radius) with stated assumptions

science.what_is: A black hole is a region where spacetime curvature is so strong that no outward light paths escape beyond the event horizon. It is defined by geometry and causal structure—not by a solid surface you could stand on.
science.event_horizon: The event horizon is a boundary in spacetime, not a material crust. Crossing it (in classical GR) is a one-way causal transition for future-directed paths; locally an infalling observer may notice nothing dramatic at that instant.
science.singularity_note: A singularity is a prediction of classical general relativity where the theory breaks down. It is not something astronomers image directly. Quantum gravity may replace this description.
science.shadow_vs_horizon: In Event Horizon Telescope images, the dark central feature—the black-hole shadow—is larger than the event horizon itself. It is shaped by light bending near the photon region and by the illuminated surroundings, reconstructed from radio interferometry.
science.accretion: Accretion disks are matter orbiting outside the horizon. Not every black hole has a bright disk. The glow comes from hot plasma and magnetic processes outside the horizon.
science.jets: Relativistic jets are launched from the magnetized accretion environment and spacetime near a spinning black hole—not from inside the event horizon.
science.photon_sphere: Near a non-rotating black hole, unstable circular photon orbits exist near about 1.5 times the Schwarzschild radius (the photon sphere). It is not a solid shell you can rest on.
science.tidal_forces: Tidal forces depend on mass and distance. At the horizon, stellar-mass black holes produce far stronger tidal gradients than supermassive ones; for large SMBHs, horizon crossing can occur before tides become locally destructive.
science.detection: Astronomers infer black holes via stellar orbits, X-ray binaries, gravitational waves from mergers, Galactic-Center dynamics, and horizon-scale EHT imaging—often combining messengers.
science.not_rubber_sheet: Rubber-sheet pictures are metaphors. Spacetime is not a fabric you can touch; measurable effects are light deflection, time dilation, and orbital dynamics.

scale_lab.label: SCHWARZSCHILD MODEL — NON-ROTATING ASSUMPTION
scale_lab.disclaimer: Rs = 2GM/c² for a non-rotating black hole. Real objects may spin; Kerr radii and shadows differ. Scales are approximate teaching aids.

examples.note: Typical order-of-magnitude stellar-mass example (not a specific named object).

approach_lab.label: ILLUSTRATIVE REGIONS — NOT EXACT KERR GEOMETRY
approach_lab.disclaimer: Ordered conceptual zones for teaching. Not a flight simulator. No free hover at the horizon. Photon sphere is not a solid shell.

regions.label: Distant space
regions.caption: Gravity is weak; light travels nearly straight; the black hole may be invisible without surrounding matter.

regions.label: Accretion region
regions.caption: If gas is present, a hot disk/corona can shine outside the horizon. Many black holes lack bright disks.

regions.label: Photon-orbit region
regions.caption: Light can skim unstable photon orbits. This region helps shape the black-hole shadow—not a solid shell.

regions.label: Event horizon
regions.caption: A causal boundary, not a surface. In classical GR, outward light cannot escape from inside.

lensing_lab.label: ILLUSTRATIVE RELATIVISTIC LENSING
lensing_lab.disclaimer: Educational deflection sketch—not a precision GR ray-tracer. Einstein-ring-like and multiple-image cues are pedagogical.

accretion_lab.label: ILLUSTRATIVE ACCRETION APPEARANCE
points: Orbital motion near the hole is fast; light travel times matter.
Gravitational redshift dims emission from deeper in the potential.
Relativistic Doppler boosting brightens the approaching side of a disk.
Light bending can make the far side of a disk appear above/below the shadow in ray-traced views.
Jets are launched outside the horizon from magnetized plasma.

tidal_lab.label: CONCEPTUAL TIDAL COMPARISON
tidal_lab.disclaimer: Uses a simple M/r³ scaling for tidal gradient teaching. Trajectory and spin matter in detail. Not a human-survival simulator.

examples.label: Stellar-mass (~10 M☉)
examples.caption: Near a stellar-mass horizon, tidal gradients are extreme—classic 'spaghettification' teaching case.

examples.label: Supermassive (~10⁶ M☉)
examples.caption: At a large SMBH horizon, local tidal gradients can be milder; horizon crossing may precede destructive tides.

detection_methods.title: Stellar orbital dynamics
detection_methods.summary: Stars whipping around an unseen compact mass (e.g. Galactic Center) reveal a central black hole.

detection_methods.title: Accretion / X-ray binaries
detection_methods.summary: A luminous accretion flow onto a compact object heavier than neutron-star limits points to a stellar-mass black hole.

detection_methods.title: Gravitational waves
detection_methods.summary: Compact-binary mergers radiate spacetime ripples detected by LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA—see the Gravitational Waves Special.

detection_methods.title: Galactic-Center orbits
detection_methods.summary: Decades of infrared astrometry of S-stars map the mass of Sgr A*.

detection_methods.title: Horizon-scale interferometry
detection_methods.summary: EHT VLBI reconstructs ring-like emission around the black-hole shadow for M87* and Sgr A*.

narration.what_is: A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity curves paths so strongly that light cannot escape beyond the event horizon. It is not a solid surface in space.
narration.horizon: The event horizon is a one-way causal boundary in classical general relativity—not a crust you could stand on. Crossing it is a geometric transition, not hitting a wall.
narration.scale: Using a simple non-rotating model, the Schwarzschild radius grows with mass. Stellar-mass holes are city-scale; supermassive holes can be larger than our Solar System.
narration.accretion: Bright rings and jets come from matter and magnetic fields outside the horizon. Many black holes are quiet without a luminous accretion flow.
narration.lensing: Near a black hole, light paths bend. Educational diagrams exaggerate this lensing; Event Horizon Telescope images reconstruct real interferometric data.
narration.tidal: Tidal forces depend on mass and distance. Small black holes can shred matter near the horizon; for huge supermassive holes, tides at the horizon can be gentler.
narration.sgr_a: Sagittarius A-star is the Milky Way's central black hole. Stars orbit an unseen mass of millions of Suns, and the Event Horizon Telescope reconstructed its shadow.
narration.m87: M87-star gave us the first horizon-scale image in 2019. The dark center is a shadow shaped by light bending—not a photograph of a black surface.
narration.detection: We find black holes through orbits, X-rays, gravitational waves, and horizon-scale radio imaging—often without ever seeing the horizon itself emit light.
narration.closing: Black holes are laboratories of extreme gravity. From stellar remnants to galactic engines, they reshape light, matter, and spacetime around them.
